instrument.full_name: Additional Protocol to the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons which may be deemed to be Excessively Injurious or to have Indiscriminate Effects (Protocol IV, entitled Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons)
instrument.depositary: Secretary-General of the United Nations (CCW Art. 10(1))
instrument.key_non_parties: States not bound by Protocol IV per the UN Treaty Collection status list (11 October 2026) include Egypt, Indonesia, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the Republic of Korea, the Syrian Arab Republic and Viet Nam. China, France, India, Israel, Pakistan, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom and the United States are all parties.
instrument.duration_clause: Protocol IV contains no duration clause. As an annexed Protocol it forms an integral part of the CCW for each party bound by it (CCW Art. 4(5)), and neither the Protocol nor the Convention sets a term. It therefore remains in force indefinitely, subject to denunciation under CCW Art. 9.
instrument.extension_clause: No extension provision is needed or stated: the Protocol has no fixed term. Its duration follows the CCW framework, which is of unlimited duration subject to denunciation (CCW Art. 9).
instrument.withdrawal_clause: Protocol IV has no withdrawal article of its own; withdrawal is governed by the CCW framework. Under CCW Art. 9(1) any High Contracting Party may denounce the Convention or any annexed Protocol by notifying the Depositary. Under Art. 9(2) denunciation takes effect one year after receipt of the notification, but a party engaged on expiry of that year in an armed conflict or occupation covered by Art. 1 remains bound until the end of the conflict or occupation and the completion of release, repatriation or re-establishment of protected persons. Denunciation of the Convention extends to all annexed Protocols (Art. 9(3)), affects only the denouncing party (Art. 9(4)), and does not affect obligations already incurred for acts committed before it takes effect (Art. 9(5)).
instrument.amendment_clause: Protocol IV has no amendment article of its own; amendment follows the CCW framework. Under CCW Art. 8(1)(a) any High Contracting Party may propose an amendment to a Protocol by which it is bound; the Depositary convenes a conference if a majority of parties, not less than eighteen, agree. Under Art. 8(1)(b) the conference may agree upon amendments, which are adopted and enter into force in the same manner as the Convention and its Protocols, and amendments to a specific Protocol may be adopted only by the parties bound by that Protocol. Amendments may also be agreed at a review conference under Art. 8(3)(a). The text does not specify a voting rule; CCW conferences operate by consensus in practice.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: Under Art. 2 of the Additional Protocol, Protocol IV enters into force as provided in CCW Art. 5(3) and (4): six months after the date by which twenty States have notified their consent to be bound, and for each later State six months after its own notification. Consent may be expressed only by States party to the CCW (Art. 4(3)-(4)). The twentieth notification (Hungary) was made on 30 January 1998, and the Protocol entered into force on 30 July 1998.
instrument.count_basis: English authentic text in the UN certified true copy (Ch_XXVI_02_ap.pdf), cross-checked against the ICRC reproduction. Six articles: two articles of the Additional Protocol (Art. 1 annexing Protocol IV; Art. 2 entry into force) and four articles of Protocol IV itself. Word count of 276 covers the full English instrument including title and article headings, counted with a whitespace tokenizer; the operative body of Protocol IV Arts. 1-4 alone is 166 words. CCW framework articles are not counted.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Laser weapons specifically designed, as their sole combat function or as one of their combat functions, to cause permanent blindness to unenhanced vision. Laser systems in general are not banned; their employment is subject to a precautions obligation.
instrument.key_provisions: Art. 1 prohibits the employment of laser weapons specifically designed, as their sole or one of their combat functions, to cause permanent blindness to unenhanced vision (the naked eye or the eye with corrective eyesight devices), and prohibits their transfer to any State or non-State entity. Art. 2 requires all feasible precautions, including training of armed forces, to avoid permanent blindness in the employment of other laser systems. Art. 3 excludes blinding as an incidental or collateral effect of legitimate military employment of laser systems, including against optical equipment. Art. 4 defines permanent blindness (irreversible, uncorrectable, seriously disabling loss of vision; visual acuity below 20/200 Snellen measured using both eyes). The Protocol does not prohibit development, production or stockpiling. Final clauses (entry into force, denunciation, amendment, depositary) derive from CCW Arts. 4-5 and 8-10.
instrument.behavior_change: Largely preventive. The Protocol banned the battlefield use and transfer of a weapon category before it had been used in combat. Human Rights Watch Arms Project findings, cited by the ICRC's Louise Doswald-Beck in 1996, identified research on blinding laser weapons in China, France, Germany, Israel, Russia and the United Kingdom and ten active or dormant US programmes. The Protocol required parties to forgo employment and transfer of such weapons and to take precautions and train forces in using other military lasers (Art. 2). It did not require destruction of existing systems or end research and production.
instrument.historical_background: Sweden brought the issue of blinding laser weapons to international attention, circulating a position paper in 1987 and later proposing a protocol during the preparations for the First CCW Review Conference. The ICRC convened four expert meetings between June 1989 and April 1991. Protocol IV was adopted by consensus at the Vienna session of the First Review Conference on 13 October 1995, under CCW Art. 8(3)(b). The ICRC described it in 1998 as only the second time in history that such a means of warfare had been prohibited before its use on the battlefield, after the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration. The ICRC customary IHL study (Rule 86) treats the prohibition of use as customary international law. (Sources: Doswald-Beck, International Review of the Red Cross, 1996; ICRC press release, 2 February 1998.)

section_provisions_md:
### Scope and core prohibition
- **Prohibition of use (Art. 1).** Parties may not employ laser weapons specifically designed, as their sole combat function or as one of their combat functions, to cause permanent blindness to unenhanced vision, meaning the naked eye or the eye with corrective eyesight devices.
- **Prohibition of transfer (Art. 1).** Parties shall not transfer such weapons to any State or non-State entity.
- The Protocol does not prohibit research, development, production or stockpiling, and contains no destruction obligation.

### Precautions and exclusions
- **Precautions (Art. 2).** In employing any laser system, parties must take all feasible precautions to avoid permanent blindness to unenhanced vision, including training of armed forces and other practical measures.
- **Incidental blinding excluded (Art. 3).** Blinding as an incidental or collateral effect of legitimate military employment of laser systems, including lasers used against optical equipment, is outside the prohibition.
- **Definition (Art. 4).** Permanent blindness is irreversible and uncorrectable loss of vision that is seriously disabling with no prospect of recovery, equivalent to visual acuity below 20/200 Snellen measured with both eyes.

### Field of application
- The Protocol applies in the situations covered by CCW Art. 1: international armed conflicts, extended to non-international armed conflicts for parties bound by the 2001 amendment to Art. 1.
- Australia, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, Sweden, the United Kingdom and others declared on consent that they will apply the Protocol in all circumstances or at all times.
- The United States filed an understanding that decisions under Art. 2 are judged on the information reasonably available at the time.

### Final clauses (derived from the CCW framework)
- **Entry into force (Additional Protocol Art. 2; CCW Art. 5(3)-(4)).** Six months after twenty States notified consent; six months after notification for each later State.
- **Participation (CCW Art. 4).** Only CCW parties may become bound; there was no signature stage.
- **Duration and withdrawal (CCW Art. 9).** No fixed term. Denunciation by notice to the Depositary takes effect after one year, deferred if the party is then engaged in an armed conflict or occupation.
- **Amendment and review (CCW Art. 8).** Amendments are proposed through the Depositary and adopted at a conference by the parties bound by the Protocol; review conferences consider the operation of all Protocols.
- **Verification and enforcement.** None specified. There are no reporting, inspection, verification or dispute-settlement provisions in the Protocol.
- **Depositary (CCW Art. 10).** The UN Secretary-General.
section_history_md:
### Origins
Sweden and Switzerland campaigned from the 1980s for a ban on anti-personnel blinding lasers, arguing that deliberate blinding causes unnecessary suffering. The ICRC convened expert meetings between 1989 and 1991, and the issue was placed before the First Review Conference of the CCW. Human Rights Watch and the ICRC reported that several states had developed prototype blinding laser systems by the mid-1990s.

### Adoption and entry into force
Protocol IV was adopted on 13 October 1995 at the Vienna session of the First Review Conference, pursuant to CCW Art. 8(3)(b). It was not opened for signature. Finland was the first State to notify consent (11 January 1996). Hungary's notification of 30 January 1998 was the twentieth, and the Protocol entered into force on 30 July 1998. The United States notified consent on 21 January 2009, with an understanding on Art. 2. As of 11 October 2026 the UN Treaty Collection lists 111 parties; the most recent are Singapore (2023) and Trinidad and Tobago (2024).

### Review
Protocol IV has no review mechanism of its own. Its operation has been considered at CCW review conferences in 2001, 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021. The ICRC describes the Protocol as the first prohibition of a weapon before its battlefield use since the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration, and its customary IHL study (Rule 86) treats the prohibition of use as customary law.

### Compliance
No party has, to available knowledge, formally alleged a violation of Protocol IV, and no denunciations are recorded. In May 2018 the US Department of Defense stated that lasers from China's base in Djibouti had caused minor eye injuries to two US C-130 pilots and lodged a demarche; China's Foreign Ministry said the accusations were inconsistent with the facts. That exchange concerned laser harassment and was not framed by either side as a Protocol IV matter.
